summary: Defines the link selection sub-option of the DHCPv4 relay agent information option. It lets a relay agent tell the server which subnet to pick addresses from, separately from the address the server should reply to. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A helper passing messages to a hotel clerk can say which floor a guest belongs on, apart from where to send the answer. This memo adds that note to DHCP.

questions: what is the dhcp link selection sub-option
dhcp link selection vs subnet selection
subtitle: A DHCP relay sub-option that names the subnet to allocate from, separate from the address used to reach the relay.

tldr.problem: The giaddr field does two jobs at once: it picks the subnet for the client and gives the server an address to reach the relay agent. That fails when the relay's address is unreachable from the server or does not exist.
tldr.mechanism: The relay adds a link-selection sub-option (sub-option code 5, length 4) to the relay-agent-information option, holding an address in the subnet the server should allocate from.
tldr.outcome: The server allocates on that subnet or another on the same link, and still replies to the address it would normally use. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 3527 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2003. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem with giaddr
sections.content:
In RFC 2131, the giaddr field holds an address that determines the subnet (and so the link) where the DHCP client lives, and it is also an address that can be used to reach the relay agent. The subnet-selection option from RFC 3011 already lets a DHCP proxy split those two roles.

The RFC describes a relay agent with a server-facing address IP x and a client-facing address IP y. Normally the relay would put IP y in giaddr, but that fails if the server cannot reach IP y. Two reasons are given: a firewall in the network element may block the server, or there may be no IP y at all, for example on a point-to-point link with a single host.

A relay can only change a client's request in two ways, through giaddr and through the relay-agent-info option. So a new sub-option of that option is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a helper who both tells the clerk which floor a guest is on and where to send the reply. If the reply address does not work, the guest gets lost. So the helper needs two separate notes.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content: The document uses the RFC 2119 key words. It defines the DHCP relay agent as a third-party agent that transfers BOOTP and DHCP messages between clients and servers on different subnets. A link is a communications facility over which nodes can talk at the layer just below IPv4, such as Ethernets, PPP links or tunnels. A subnet is a routable address range, and it may be one of several that exist on a link at the same time.
sections.plainLanguage: A link is like a whole floor of a building, and a subnet is one hallway on that floor. A floor can have several hallways.

sections.title: The Link-Selection Sub-Option
sections.content:
A relay agent uses the sub-option when it needs the subnet or link for a client to differ from the address the server should use to talk to the relay. The sub-option carries a single IP address inside the subnet. The subnet is found by ANDing any address on it with the subnet mask. The server also considers other subnets on the same link, as it does for giaddr in RFC 2131.

The format is one octet of sub-option code (5), one octet of length (4) and four octets of address. In these scenarios the relay adds the sub-option whenever it sets giaddr, so on all messages relayed to the server.
sections.plainLanguage: The note is tiny: a label, a size, and one address that sits in the right hallway.

sections.title: How Relays and Servers Behave
sections.content:
When allocating an address and the sub-option is present, the server MUST allocate on the subnet it names, or on a subnet on the same link. If the server supports the sub-option it MUST NOT offer an address outside that subnet or link.

If a packet has both a RFC 3011 subnet-selection option and a link-selection sub-option, the link-selection sub-option MUST be used in preference. The address to which the server sends its reply MUST be the same as it would choose without the sub-option.

A relay using the sub-option MUST assume the server supports it, and MUST NOT behave differently depending on whether the sub-option appears in the server's response. Administrators should use administrative techniques to ensure such a relay only sends to servers that support it. Servers need no other changes; for example, handling of a DHCPDISCOVER for an unknown subnet continues unchanged.
sections.plainLanguage: The clerk must give the guest a room on the named floor, but still sends the answer to the usual place. The helper must trust that the clerk understood.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points to the DHCP attack discussion in RFC 2131 and the authentication work in RFC 3118. Because subnet selection already exists in RFC 3011, it says this sub-option raises no fundamental new security issues beyond those.

It does note that either option lets a malicious client mount a more complete address-pool exhaustion attack, since it is no longer limited to its local subnet. The sub-option gives some minor extra protection: a trusted relay agent that supports the relay-agent-info option MUST discard a packet with a zero giaddr and a relay-agent-info option arriving on an untrusted circuit.
sections.plainLanguage: A sneaky guest might ask for rooms on floors they should not use up. The helper is told to throw away notes that arrive from places it does not trust.

sections.title: IANA Assignment
sections.content:
IANA assigned the value 5 from the DHCP Relay Agent sub-options space defined in RFC 3046 for the link-selection sub-option.

The document is based largely on the text of the RFC 3011 subnet-selection option, with only minimal modifications.
sections.plainLanguage: The sub-option got its own official number, 5, so everyone uses the same label.

fields.name: Subnet IP address
fields.desc: An address in the subnet to allocate from.
